HEADLINE: MCN partners with SAS for new data platform
TEXT:
Multi-Channel Network has partnered with the world's largest privately held software business SAS to develop a new data platform for targeted advertising across linear television and digital properties.

MCN chief data officer Mark Brandon said the new platform, which will launch in 2018, is designed to pull together all the business's data sources across TV, online, mobile, out-of-home and agency and will act as the "central nervous system" for the Foxtel, Fox Sports and Network Ten joint venture.

"We've been looking for some time to find a partner that can take us to the next level in data terms," Mr Brandon told The Australian Financial Review.

"We believe the period we're in now, where media meets data, it's an interim state, meaning we've come from a place but we haven't completed the journey yet."

MCN, which runs advertising sales for Foxtel and Ten, hopes the new platform, SIA, will allow advertisers to target single consumers across all media platforms.

"Building on our pioneering work with Landmark and Programmatic TV, SIA evolves our sophisticated media data, targeting and trading capabilities. The platform will redefine how integrated media campaigns are developed, delivered and analysed in Australia," Mr Brandon, former commercial director of Britain's Virgin Media, said.

MCN and SAS began development on SIA earlier in 2017 and are going through test cases for the rest of the year with the rollout pencilled in for next year.

"SIA is, in turn, the brain behind the addressable TV. What we're seeing so far we like."

Addressable TV enables the serving of ads unique to each screen and consumer based on data collected about that person. MCN is also able to use data collected via Foxtel set-top boxes, which is also overlaid with Quantium data from Woolworths' Everyday Rewards cards and National Bank of Australia credit and debit cards.

SAS Australian and New Zealand vice-president David Bowie said SIA represented a major advance in the use of technology to better service the advertising industry.

"The adoption of SAS will enable MCN to gain maximum productivity from its numerous and highly diverse data sources, for the benefit of its clients," he said.

Mr Brandon said MCN chose to work with SAS after a long search for the best partner who could help the business address data transactions in a highly privacy compliant, premium and intelligent way.

The complex search included exam questions to answer and practical data problems where potential partners needed to come up with solutions.

"We chose a provider that came in front in all those tests and had the advanced analytics capacity level," Mr Brandon said.

HEADLINE: Telstra taps Laing on Fox Sports merger
TEXT:
Former Nine Entertainment managing director Amanda Laing has signed on with Telstra to help the telecommunications giant work through the merger of Foxtel and Fox Sports.

Sources said Ms Laing, who left Nine earlier this year, is consulting with the telco which is seeking to take advantage of her media expertise.

It is understood Ms Laing is working with Telstra group executive of new businesses Cynthia Whelan, who is also Foxtel chairman, and began in September. Telstra confirmed it is working with Ms Laing on the merger.

Telstra is keen to make sure it sets its media strategy up correctly, with content playing a key role in the future of telecommunications.

Ms Laing, whose first stop after leaving Nine was an executive leadership course at Stanford University in California, played a pivotal role in Nine's NRL, Cricket Australia, affiliate agreements and sat on the board of Stan, Nine's 50-50 joint-venture subscription video on-demand service with Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review.

She worked across various businesses at Nine over her 18-year career at the network, including general counsel for ACP Magazines – which was sold to Bauer Media in 2012 for $525 million – general counsel for the entire Nine group, commercial director and in 2015 was promoted to managing director.

Once considered a potential replacement for former Nine chief executive David Gyngell, Ms Laing also helped the broadcaster with its 2013 initial public offering, the purchase of WIN Corp's stations in Adelaide and Perth, Nine's exit from its Microsoft joint-venture, and its affiliate agreement with Southern Cross Austereo.

Telstra and News Corporation, who both own 50 per cent of Foxtel, will merge the pay television provider with News Corp-wholly owned Fox Sports, as revealed by the Financial Review in August. News Corp will own 65 per cent of the merged entity, with Telstra owning the remaining 35 per cent.

Telstra has also flagged it will sell down its stake in the combined company when it is listed on the Australian Securities Exchange.

However, the listing is understood to be a long-term plan for the combined entity as it, like many other media companies, seeks to implement a new growth strategy in a challenging environment.

The short-term plan would not be to float the business as Foxtel deals with a number of headwinds and chief executive Peter Tonagh is given time to implement its subscription video on-demand strategy with Foxtel Now, which launched in July.

Foxtel subscriber numbers fell to 2.8 million as of June 30 this year, down from 2.9 million compared with the prior corresponding period. News Corp said the fall was primarily related to the shutdown of Presto.

Foxtel's profit dropped to $US59 million, compared with $US180 million in the previous year. However, this was largely related to a $US58 million loss due to a write-down in its investment in Network Ten, which has gone into receivership and has been bought by US studio CBS, and $US53 million in losses from the closing of Presto.

An integrated Fox Sports and Foxtel is expected to be a more attractive business because of the value of live sports in Australia – Fox Sports has secured long-term agreements for rugby union, NRL, AFL and the A-League.

HEADLINE: Stan hits $100 million revenue run rate
TEXT:
Subscription video on-demand service Stan has hit a revenue run rate of $100 million as the near-two-year-old business pushes towards being cashflow break-even in the second half of 2017-18.

The streaming joint-venture, which is 50-50 owned by Nine Entertainment and Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review, launched in January 2015 and has amassed more than 800,000 active subscribers, second in the SVOD space only to global giant Netflix.

The Australian streaming market has exploded and contracted in a short space of time. Stan has seen off local competitors Presto, a joint-venture between Foxtel and Seven West Media, which folded in 2016, and Quickflix. Global e-commerce giant Amazon launched its streaming service Prime in late 2016, as revealed by the Financial Review.

Over 2016-17, Stan grew revenue by 260 per cent and chief executive Mike Sneesby said the business remained on track to be cashflow break-even in the second half of 2017-18.

"Zero to $100 million run rate in two years is a great milestone," he said. "The strategy we've had is a consistent road map of strong exclusive programming from Hollywood studios, Showtime and our own original productions. This year we're sitting at around 35 exclusives and originals."

Run rate refers to financial data that indicates what money is coming into the business at a particular point in time and then annualised. For example, if Stan stood still for the next 12 months and stayed on its $100 million revenue run rate, it would be bringing in roughly $8.3 million per month.

However, Mr Sneesby said he expected Stan's revenue and subscriber base to continue to grow with the next hit coming from the seasonal high growth periods of November, December, January.

Credit Suisse analyst Fraser McLeish wrote in a recent note to clients Stan had the potential to keep growing as the SVOD category gets bigger in Australia.

"US SVOD penetration is now around 65 per cent and we expect Australia to reach a similar level over time [vs circa 20-25 per cent currently]," he said.

Mr McLeish has valued Stan between $400 million and $600 million, and sees the potential for CBS – which has a content agreement with Stan and has bought free-to-air broadcaster Network Ten – to take a stake in the streaming service rather than going it alone in Australia.

"We believe that once CBS takes full ownership of Ten and starts to consider its streaming options, there is a reasonable chance that it may look to acquire a stake in Stan. Stan owns the rights to CBS' key Showtime content and the two companies already have close ties," he said.

"CBS needs a streaming strategy for the Australian market and we believe that it will face some major challenges in trying to grow its CBS All-Access service organically in Australia."

Mr McLeish said existing contracts with Stan for CBS' Showtime content, and a number of other deals locking up key shows, such as Big Bang Theory on Nine, Criminal Minds on Seven and Star Trek with Netflix, could mean the US studio would have to wait a long time before being able to offer a full suite of shows if it pursues streaming alone.

"We believe that having CBS as an ownership partner would be a major positive for Stan as: 1) Stan would effectively secure the longer term rights for the Showtime brand and content; 2) CBS would be able to bring other content to the platform; 3) CBS would bring marketing power as it could promote Stan using the Ten Network."

HEADLINE: Sex, drugs and Bitcoin
TEXT:
A research project led by an Australian expert in detecting insider trading has quantified the scale of illegal activity financed through the world's largest digital currency, Bitcoin.

About a third of Bitcoin users are using the anonymous digital currency for nefarious activities, according to the research titled, Sex, Drugs and Bitcoin written by Sean Foley, Talis Putnins and Jonathan Karlsen.

They found that 34 million to 36 million of the 106 million users of Bitcoin have been using the digital currency for illegal activity.

The research tracks illegal activity going back to 2009. One of the more interesting findings is that illegal activity peaked in about July 2014 and has been trending down since.

Foley told Chanticleer this was not unexpected given that just about every market in the world usually started with a bunch of cowboys pushing the legal limits. Markets usually evolve to a point where the illegal activity is shaken out as regulators step in.

The concept of regulation of Bitcoin will blow the minds of those who are true believers in currency that has no central controlling manager and always guarantees anonymity.

In the process of conducting their research, Foley, Putnins and Karlsen have developed novel methods for identifying illegal activity in Bitcoin. They say that much of this research can be transferable to any public blockchain technology.

That is significant because stock exchanges around the world are considering using the blockchain technologies that underpin Bitcoin for settlement of equities trading. These technologies could ultimately be used in any industry that involves transactions between two or more parties.

Bitcoin is celebrated for its anonymity but the blockchain technology means there is a record for every transaction that has ever occurred. This unique quality was a huge benefit to the research by Foley, Putnins and Karlsen.

"Recent and ongoing seizures of Bitcoin by law enforcement agencies, combined with the public nature of the blockchain, provide us with a unique laboratory within which to analyse the illegal ecosystem that has evolved in the Bitcoin network," they said in their research proposal.

"Although individual identities are masked by the pseudo-anonymity of a 33 character alpha-numeric address, the public nature of the blockchain allows us to link bitcoin transactions to individual "users" (market participants), identify users that had bitcoin seized by authorities, and analyse the network of who trades with whom.

"The Bitcoin seizures therefore provide us with a sample of users known to be involved in illegal activity from which we can infer or estimate other Bitcoin users involved in illegal activity.

"Our first approach to doing so is by analysing the trade networks of users known to be involved in illegal activity.

"Our second approach is to exploit characteristics that can distinguish between users involved in illegal activity and those involved in legal activity using detection controlled estimation models.

"For example, for each Bitcoin user we are able to measure the extent to which they take actions to conceal their identity and trading records. Using these innovative tools, we are able to approximate the size of the black market economy facilitated by this new technology, and characterise the nature of illegal activity involving Bitcoin."

The starting point for the research was a bunch of questions. These were: What fraction of bitcoin trading activity and holdings is associated with illegal activity? What are the characteristics of illegal activity using bitcoin? How do the networks of illegal trade differ from those of legal trade? How do bitcoin users involved in illegal activity differ from those involved in legal activity? How do transactions associated with illegal activity differ from legal transactions? How can illegal activity be detected in bitcoin, or on a public blockchain more generally?

In seeking to answer these questions the researchers had to spend a reasonable amount of time on the dark web, also known as the "darknet".

"The darknet is a network like the internet, but can be accessed only through particular communications protocols that provide greater anonymity than the internet," the research paper says.

"The darknet contains online marketplaces, much like eBay, but with anonymous communications, which also makes these marketplaces less accessible than online stores on the internet.

"Darknet marketplaces are particularly popular for trading goods and services where buyers and sellers want to conceal their identities, for example, illegal goods and services. The darknet is estimated to contain approximately 30,000 domains."

The paper says that a user who wants to buy goods or services on a darknet marketplace must first acquire digital currency (typically from an online exchange or broker) and then deposit this in an address belonging to the darknet marketplace (often termed a "hot wallet").

The other element that has facilitated illegal activity online involving Bitcoin is TOR (The Onion Router).

"By providing an anonymous, digital method of payment, bitcoin did for darknet marketplaces what Paypal did for eBay— provide a reliable, scalable, and convenient payment mechanism," the paper says.

"What was also required, however, was an anonymous way of hosting and accessing those illegal marketplaces.

"This issue is solved through the use of TOR, originally developed by the US Navy. TOR hides the IP address of internet traffic through 'onion routing', which obfuscates the path (and hence IP) of a message sent between two clients by routing the message through several nodes in the TOR network."

The groundbreaking work has gained in-principle acceptance for publication in a leading international finance journal early next year. It is being undertaken in collaboration with the Sydney-based Capital Markets Cooperative Research Centre.

The research is designed to help securities regulators understand the size of the task they face in attempting to monitor and regulate what is fast becoming an accepted asset class for institutional investors.

It is extraordinary but true that Bitcoin has quickly evolved from being the preferred digital currency for illegal purchases on the dark web to becoming one of the fastest-growing asset classes in the world.

There is a plan to have Bitcoin futures traded on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange - one of the world's largest options and futures exchanges.

We know from various actions by police in the United States, Asia, Australia and Europe that Bitcoin has been used on the dark web to buy drugs, avoid capital controls, launder money and pay for computer hacking.

The recent global Wanna Crypt computer hacking attack demanded payment of ransom in Bitcoins.

The most famous user of Bitcoin for illicit purposes was the Silk Road drug site. When it was busted by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation about $4 million in Bitcoin was seized.

But these illegal activities have to be put in the context of the potential value that may accrue to business and government from the use of the anonymous blockchain technologies that underpin Bitcoin and its spin-offs Bitcoin Gold and Bitcoin Cash.

A form of blockchain is being talked about as a possible solution for the settlement of equities trading in Australia and elsewhere.

TONY BOYD

HEADLINE: Anchorage restocks war chest
TEXT:
Anchorage Capital Partners can start hunting for companies in need of TLC having successfully raised $350 million for its third turnaround fund.

Street Talk can reveal the Phil Cave and Callen O'Brien-led private equity firm has closed Anchorage Capital Partners Fund III, three months after launching the cash call.

An announcement is expected on Thursday. Street Talk flagged in September that the Sydney-based turn-around specialist was on track for a final close.

"ACP III was considerably oversubscribed, with demand exceeding the fundraising target, attributable to continued strong support from existing investors combined with significant interest of new investors," Anchorage managing director Simon Woodhouse told this column.

It is understood over 40 per cent of commitments were sourced from Australian institutions, while offshore limited partners provided the balance.

Anchorage makes controlling investments in underperforming Australasian and south-east Asian businesses, which have enterprise values between $30 million and $250 million.

Its exits which made good returns for investors include Singapore-based First Engineering, Golden Circle, Burger King and Dick Smith Holdings.

The firm's most recent transactions include a deal to acquire facility maintenance provider TJS Services and an investment in Bapcor Ltd's industrial waste services unit, Contract Resources.

HEADLINE: Globalvia, CIMIC tap advisers as Westconnex sale rolls on
TEXT:
The battle lines are still being drawn as parties position to acquire a majority stake in New South Wales' $16.8 billion roads project WestConnex.

Street Talk understands European toll-road and railway giant Globalvia has tapped HSBC for advice, while JPMorgan is separately working with ASX-listed contractor and construction company CIMIC.

The pair joins a long list of potential suitors, many of whom are in talks with each other and other potential partners, as they seek to form bidding groups. It also ensures a busy time for investment banks, with just about every transport infrastructure adviser in the country securing a role.

Locally, Transurban is seen as the strongest contender with the trio of Morgan Stanley, UBS, and Macquarie Capital on hand to advise.

Up for grabs is 50.1 per cent in Sydney Motorway Corporation, which was established to build and own the motorways project.

Expressions of interest were submitted earlier this month and the first-round bid phase is due to start in December. Under the current time-table indicative offers will be lobbed in mid-February.

Working in Globalvia's favour is that it manages 28 projects in eight different countries, including the US, specialising in highways and railways.

That is likely to sit well with the NSW government's search for experienced operators and owners of toll roads.

Among deals this year, Globalvia last month completed the acquisition of 100 per cent of the A23 motorway Beira Interior (Scutvias) of Portugal.

This column revealed Globalvia's WestConnex interest in July when representatives from the company were in Sydney meeting with government officials, industry players and bankers.

The company's shareholders are Canadian pension investor OPTrust, UK pension fund giant Universities Superannuation Scheme and Dutch pension fund manager PGGM.

Also in the WestConnex contest - flanked by their respective advisers - are Cintra/Plenary Group-backed Netflow, CP2 and Spanish road operator Abertis, local firm IFM Investors, and separately Shandong Hi-Speed Group and its subsidiary.

HEADLINE: Transurban hasn't given up hope of pre-Xmas deal
TEXT:
Transurban Group investors may be well advised to keep some cash on the sidelines this Christmas, with the toll-road company mulling a share issue to help pay for a $5.5 billion expansion project in Melbourne.

The project is the West Gate Tunnel, which Transurban is seeking to develop in partnership with the Victorian government. The new tunnel received environmental and planning approval this week, which moved it up the chain to the Victorian roads minister for approval, and later cabinet.

Transurban has long told investors it is seeking to have the project approved and reach financial close by the end of this year. And it is understood that timetable has not changed.

Financial close would trigger a $3.5 billion to $4 billion funding commitment for Transurban, split between debt and equity.

While the toll-road company does not have to write a big cheque on day one, it has been working on funding options all year and is expected to move sooner rather than later.

So expectations on equities desks are building of a $2 billion-odd equity raising heading into Christmas, provided the company can clear that final government hurdle. House advisers Morgan Stanley and UBS would be expected to handle the deal.

Transurban chairman Lindsay Maxsted has not shied away from discussing the potential raising with investors.

At the annual general meeting last month, Maxsted made it abundantly clear that Transurban would continue to fund big expansion projects like the West Gate Tunnel with equity raisings. And it's no secret he prefers to use entitlement offers over quicker but arguably less fair structures, including institutional placements.

Entitlement offers are tricky at this time of year. Retail shareholders are often distracted, increasing the likelihood of a large shortfall and risk for underwriters.

But they have been done before.

Transurban has even done it. The $26 billion toll-roads giant launched a $1.025 billion rights issue on November 24, 2015, to fund its acquisition of the AirportLink M7 toll road in Brisbane via broker UBS.

Listed infrastructure player APA Group went even later in 2014, with a $1.839 billion rights issue that launched on December 10. That deal, underwritten by Morgan Stanley, Macquarie Capital and Deutsche Bank, ran two timetables for the retail offer - allowing retail investors to accept early, by December 19, or by January 15.

HEADLINE: Offshore giants mobilise deal teams for Suncorp's life unit
TEXT:
Australia's life insurance industry is set to see a pitched battle between financial services giants from the East and the West.

Street Talk can reveal US behemoth American International Group and Japan's Dai-ichi Life are among parties expected to submit indicative offers for Suncorp's up-for-sale life insurance unit by Thursday's deadline.

It is understood New York-listed AIG is working with JPMorgan's corporate finance team, just two months after the investment bank helped Commonwealth Bank of Australia navigate the sale of its Australian and New Zealand life insurance units to AIA Group for $3.8 billion.

AIG already has an Australian business focused on consumer and commercial insurance products, with more than 300 employees and $304 million in net written premium in 2015. It is part of the US-listed AIG, which has a $US54 billion market capitalisation.

Should AIG make it through to the second round of Suncorp's sale process, it would have to be considered a strong contender given its size and scale.

Meanwhile, Dai-ichi Life, which acquired Australian life insurance specialist TAL in 2010, has had long-time adviser Greenhill Australia in its corner as it prepares its first-round bid.

The Japanese insurer has been an active participant in local life auctions this year. It ran the ruler over CBA's Sovereign, New Zealand's largest life insurance business, and was also involved in the auction for ANZ Banking Group's wealth unit.

Suncorp is likely to be a more manageable bite for Dai-ichi. While the unit is on the books for about $1 billion, Citigroup analysts note that is nearly 30-times what profit the division made in the 2017 financial year excluding the impact of one-off items.

The Nomura and Luminis Partners-advised auction has also had to compete for attention with similar processes from ANZ and wealth giant AMP which are both seeking to sell businesses that are bigger [and arguably of better quality] than Suncorp's.

At its full-year results, Suncorp reported a 50 per cent drop in life insurance net profit to $34 million. Underlying profit was unchanged at $53 million but in-force annual premium and total new life business declined.

Elsewhere, as first reported by Street Talk, Westpac Banking Corp's sale of its infrastructure arm Hastings Funds Management has hit a roadblock.

Utilities Trust of Australia - which Hastings runs and accounts for about half of the firm's assets under management - has put its management rights up for tender. Investor sources said UTA is expected to exclude Hastings from the request for proposal.

It comes just one month after UK-based Northill Capital agreed to buy Westpac's stake in Hastings for $150 million to $160 million.

HEADLINE: Clare zags with new fund
TEXT:
Former Westpac Banking Corp executive Peter Clare is ramping things up at marketplace lender Zagga, which he co-founded with former Real Home Loans boss Alan Greenstein.

Street Talk understands Zagga is raising a new fund that it will tip into loans for customers using its platform.

The direct and technology-based lending industry does, however, appear to be getting crowded as a string of players look to chip away at the market share of established lenders and banks.

Zagga connects wholesale investors with borrowers via an online platform and has algorithmic matching of borrower credit risk with the investor's appetite for risk.

While the new fund is not targeting a hard close, or specific amount, sources suggested a raising in the order of $20 million to $50 million in the medium term would be viewed as a good outcome.

The fund is said to target a net 6.5 per cent annual return for wholesale investors. Since leaving Westpac, Clare has also popped up as a senior adviser to Moelis Australia, is chairman of ASX-listed Change Financial and a director of Scottish Pacific.

Elsewhere, as first reported by this column, law firm Clifford Chance has lured local Herbert Smith Freehills mergers partner Mark Currell.

Currell - who has advised on deals for KKR & Co and Blackstone - focuses on private equity, special situations and restructuring.

HEADLINE: Marriage bill clears Senate
TEXT:
Conservatives will continue their fight to bolster religious protections in same-sex marriage legislation when deliberations shift to the House of Representatives next week, despite suffering a thumping defeat in the Senate on Wednesday.

Applause erupted and tears were shed as senators voted 43 to 12 to allow gay couples to wed, the first time one of Federal Parliament's chambers have passed a same-sex marriage bill.

But former prime minister Tony Abbott said it was "disappointing" the government did not fight more to strengthen religious protections and parental rights, while Nationals backbenchers Andrew Broad and George Christensen accused Malcolm Turnbull of lacking leadership over the issue.

Despite moderate Liberals joining Labor MPs and crossbenchers to steamroll the amendments in the Senate, opponents will regroup and hold a phone hook-up to plot strategy ahead of the House of Representatives return on Monday.

While they know they cannot stop gay marriage being legalised, and many lower house MPs have pledged not to block its passage, one Liberal said as a matter of principle they needed to keep fighting. "We've got to try because nearly 40 per cent of the population voted 'No'," the MP told The Australian Financial Review.

"It's disappointing they didn't get enough support in the Senate but many Coalition members will support amendments."

Mr Abbott said he expected amendments similar to those moved by backbench Liberal senators David Fawcett and James Paterson would be introduced into the House of Representatives. He said it was a pity former attorney-general Philip Ruddock's inquiry into religious freedom would not report before the same-sex marriage vote and pointed out both Mr Turnbull and Opposition Leader Bill Shorten had committed to protecting religious freedoms during the postal vote period.

"It's disappointing that Shorten didn't give his own members freedom to cross the floor and it's disappointing that the government hasn't done more to ensure freedom of religion is protected at the same time same-sex marriage is passed," he said.

Mr Broad told the ABC "there's been a complete lack of leadership" by Mr Turnbull in ensuring a bill acceptable to conservatives was prepared, a view endorsed by Mr Christensen. "A true leader would have sought to capture the will of the people and protect freedoms, not this hands-off approach," Mr Christensen said on Twitter.

Mr Turnbull tried to head off the criticism by saying voters "do not expect politicians to be talking about each other". "They expect them to be focused on the big issues ... national security, keeping Australians safe. Trade. Jobs. Employment," he said.

Senator Dean Smith said the resounding victory showed what could happen when senators put aside partisan differences. "We have seen in this debate how our Parliament is meant to work," he said.

Labor Senate leader Penny Wong said it was a day of celebration. "It says to so many Australians: this Parliament, this country, accept you for who you are. Your love is not lesser and nor are you. It says you are one of us," she said.
